title: Initial Results on Legal Agent Benchmark: A First Look at Frontier Model Performance on Long-Horizon Legal-Agent Work
author: Niko Grupen · Gabe Pereyra · Julio Pereyra

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source accepts task-specific, end-to-end evaluation and materially develops the proposition through LAB’s strict all-pass grading, showing that frontier models complete fewer than 10% of legal tasks despite potential partial success. It also extends evaluation beyond quality scores to practice-area variation, cost, latency and agent trajectories.
qs: We scored each task under LAB’s all-pass standard, where a task counts as passing only if every required rubric criterion passes.

From this analysis, three meaningful trends have emerged:  -  Legal work is far from saturated by frontier models**: Under our strict all-pass standard, the frontier models we evaluated complete less than 10% of tasks end-to-end in aggregate.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that legal-AI capability is jagged and inadequate for general autonomous competence. It materially extends the selective-deployment proposition by recommending task-specific routing across multiple model families and by adding cost and latency as necessary production criteria alongside quality.
qs: Maximizing agent performance on a real legal workload requires understanding which model family best matches the task at hand.
Production agent deployments need more than a high benchmark score.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: Harvey’s LAB results directly support the synthesis: strict all-required-criteria grading yields under-10% end-to-end completion despite frontier-model capabilities, while aggregate scores mask substantial practice-area variation. Its cost, latency and agent-trace observations add supporting operational context without changing the cluster’s framing.

Aggregating across all of them into one all-pass number masks that task diversity.

kp.k: Strict benchmarking finds low end-to-end legal task completion
kp.d: In their May 26, 2026 report, Harvey authors Niko Grupen, Gabe Pereyra and Julio Pereyra report results on a hold-out evaluation set mirroring the practice areas and task distribution of the open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB). A task passes only when every expert-curated rubric criterion passes, covering facts, conclusions, citations, structure and analytical moves. They grade runs multiple times across model families and average results to address grader bias. Evaluated frontier models complete less than 10% of tasks end-to-end in aggregate under this standard; the authors interpret this as evidence that frontier models cannot yet deliver complete legal work product.
qs: We scored each task under LAB’s all-pass standard, where a task counts as passing only if every required rubric criterion passes.
To prevent grader bias, we grade agent runs multiple times across model families and average the results.
Under our strict all-pass standard, the frontier models we evaluated complete less than 10% of tasks end-to-end in aggregate.

kp.k: Overall model leadership still entails very low pass rates
kp.d: The reported overall hold-out all-pass scores are Claude Opus 4.7 at 7.1%, Sonnet 4.6 at 5.4%, Opus 4.6 at 4.2%, GPT-5.5 at 2.1%, and Gemini 3.5 Flash at 0.8%. The authors describe a rapidly improving frontier that remains inadequate under their strict review standard, rather than treating leaderboard leadership as evidence of reliable legal-task completion.
qs: Claude Opus 4.7 leads at 7.1%, with Sonnet 4.6 at 5.4%, Opus 4.6 at 4.2%, GPT-5.5 at 2.1%, and Gemini 3.5 Flash at 0. 8% to round out the major model families we’ve evaluated thus far.
Read against the strict review standard legal work actually demands, these numbers describe a frontier that is improving rapidly but is not yet good enough.

kp.k: Practice-area variation motivates multi-model legal agents
kp.d: Across three equal-sized practice-area groupings, different models lead: GPT-5.5 in regulated and emerging-company work involving retrieval-heavy research; Opus 4.7 in corporate transactions and funds work emphasizing synthesis and analysis; and Sonnet 4.6 in privacy, tax and private-client work emphasizing structured statutory and regulatory comparison. The authors characterize this as jagged intelligence and recommend matching models to tasks. Their statement that the strongest production deployments will be multi-model is a prospective deployment judgment, distinct from the measured rankings.
qs: To understand model performance across practice areas, we created three equal-sized practice-area groupings and re-ranked the same four model families inside each one.
GPT-5.5 leads in the regulated and emerging-company groups, where retrieval-heavy research is a larger part of the work.
Opus 4.7 leads the corporate transactions and funds categories, where synthesis and analytical work dominates.
The strongest production agent deployments will be multi-model from the start.

kp.k: Quality gains carry substantial cost and latency trade-offs
kp.d: Opus 4.7, the highest-scoring configuration, is also the most expensive and slowest evaluated, costing about $50.90 per task with roughly 22 minutes of wall-clock time. GPT-5.5 is approximately 3x cheaper, while Gemini 3.5 Flash produces a draft in under six minutes, nearly 4x faster, but both score below Opus 4.7 on this hold-out. The authors argue that deployability depends jointly on quality, customer spending limits and acceptable waiting times, not benchmark quality alone.
qs: Opus 4.7, the highest-performing model by all-pass score, is the most expensive and slowest configuration in the set, at about $50.90 per task and roughly 22 minutes of wall-clock time.
GPT-5.5 is approximately 3x cheaper and, in terms of latency, Gemini 3.5 Flash returns a draft in under six minutes (nearly 4x faster), but both land below the all-pass leader on this holdout.
They need a high score inside a budget that a customer will tolerate: the dollars they will spend per task, and the time they will wait for a draft.

kp.k: Agent trajectories reveal different legal-work strengths
kp.d: The evaluated agents use six available actions—Read, Search, Execute, Write, Validate and Edit—and each run records their sequence. The authors associate Opus 4.7's more self-corrective drafting, checking and revision behavior with higher drafting-task scores, and GPT-5.5's heavier search and broader document coverage with stronger research-task scores. They advocate examining behavior alongside final scores to understand performance in high-stakes legal work. The validation described here is an agent's own checking step, not human verification.
qs: In addition to a scored rubric, every LAB run produces an agent trace that captures how the agent sequenced these actions to produce its final deliverable.

Opus 4.7 agents, for example, are the most visibly self-corrective, spending more of their trajectory on drafting than other models on average, and frequently re-checking, validating, and revising their own outputs before finishing work.
GPT-5.5 has by far the largest search segment of any family, running document search more heavily than other models and covering a wider breadth of documents on average.

kp.k: Self-correction has the strongest positive behavioral association
kp.d: The trace analysis reports an average 0.8 point all-pass improvement for post-draft validation and a 1.5 point improvement for revising after checking, the strongest positive pattern identified. Drafting without later validation or revision is associated with scores falling by 1.2 points on average. These are reported relationships between observed behaviors and outcomes; the authors frame checking and substantive revision as recognizable features of competent associate work.
qs: Agents that run a validation or review step after drafting, rather than treating the first draft as final, see a 0.8 point average improvement in all-pass score.
Agents that close this revise-after-check loop improve all-pass scores by 1.5 points on average.
Agents that draft but skip later validation or revision perform materially worse, with all-pass scores falling by 1.2 points on average.
Self-correction is the strongest positive signal.

kp.k: Context gathering and structured analysis correlate with better outcomes
kp.d: The authors report a 0.4 point average all-pass improvement when agents build broad context before drafting, exemplified by >90% document coverage during research. Targeted retrieval, code- or shell-based structured analysis, and returning to source documents after drafting each correspond to a 0.3 point average improvement. These findings support the authors' account of stronger legal-agent workflows as gathering context, locating missing facts, analyzing evidence and grounding drafts in the matter record.
qs: When the agent builds broad matter context before producing work product — e.g. achieving >90% document coverage in the research phase — all-pass scores improve by 0.4 points on average.
Agents that search the matter file during the run can locate facts across the broader corpus instead of relying only on initially opened documents, improving all-pass scores by 0.3 points on average.
When agents use code or shell tools to compute, parse, or verify evidence, they turn parts of the legal task into a more systematic analysis step, improving all-pass scores by 0.3 points on average.
Agents that return to source documents after drafting appear to check or correct the work product against the underlying evidence, improving all-pass scores by 0.3 points on average.

kp.k: Extensive parallel tool use may undermine task performance
kp.d: Five or more tool calls in a single turn are associated with a 0.5 point decrease in all-pass score. The authors suggest, rather than establish, that broad search without sufficient direction adds noise and creates workstreams that become difficult to synthesize.
qs: High parallel tool use — i.e. five or more tool calls in a single turn — can cover ground quickly, but is associated with a 0.5 point decrease in all-pass score, suggesting that broad search without enough direction may add noise.

kp.k: Reliable legal agents require broader research and benchmarking
kp.d: The authors identify long-horizon task execution, domain-knowledge transfer across legal specialties, and cost and latency improvements as research priorities rather than accomplished capabilities. They plan richer task families, additional practice areas, adjacent professional-service workflows and longer-context matters, alongside collaboration with model providers. They also announce a partnership with Artificial Analysis to scale evaluation and publish a regularly updated leaderboard, positioning trajectory analysis as important to interpreting future progress.
qs: Closing the gap between today’s frontier and reliable legal-agent performance is going to require sustained research across multiple fronts: how agents handle long-horizon professional tasks, how they internalize the domain knowledge that transfers across legal sub-domains, and how they deliver that performance inside the cost and latency budgets production deployments actually require.
Richer task families covering more practice areas, adjacent professional-service workflows beyond legal, and longer-context matters.
We are partnering with Artificial Analysis to scale up LAB evaluation and publish a regularly-updated leaderboard as new model launches arrive.
We cannot improve what we cannot interpret, and on long-horizon professional work the right unit of measurement is the trajectory as much as the final score.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Grupen, Gabe Pereyra and Julio Pereyra argue that current frontier agents cannot yet reliably complete complex legal work end-to-end; production performance depends on task-specific model selection, cost and latency constraints, and agents' research and self-correction behaviors.
pts.d: The Harvey authors report that all evaluated frontier models complete fewer than 10% of tasks under LAB's strict all-pass standard, interpreting this as evidence that frontier intelligence cannot yet deliver complete legal work product. They describe capabilities as uneven across practice areas and predict that the strongest production deployments will use multiple models. GPT-5.5 leads the regulated and emerging-company groupings, Opus 4.7 leads corporate transactions and funds, and Sonnet 4.6 leads privacy, tax and private-client work. They also argue that benchmark quality alone is insufficient for deployment: customer tolerance for monetary cost and waiting time matters. Their behavioral analysis associates broad research, targeted retrieval, structured analysis, grounding against source documents, and especially revision after checking with higher scores; drafting without review and excessive parallel tool use are associated with lower scores. They compare these successful behaviors with competent associate workflows, without claiming that agents can replace associates. Looking ahead, they argue that reliable legal agents require sustained research into long-horizon work, domain-knowledge transfer, and cost and latency, and predict increasing importance for behavioral interpretability.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw on Harvey's LAB holdout benchmarking, configuration-level cost and latency measurements, and qualitative and quantitative analysis of agent action traces.
pts.d: The authors evaluate a holdout set mirroring the public LAB task distribution, using expert-curated rubrics and an all-pass rule requiring every criterion to pass. They report grading runs multiple times across model families and averaging results to address grader bias. Overall scores are Opus 4.7 at 7.1%, Sonnet 4.6 at 5.4%, Opus 4.6 at 4.2%, GPT-5.5 at 2.1%, and Gemini 3.5 Flash at 0.8%. Three equal-sized practice-area groupings support the claim of uneven model strengths. Opus 4.7 costs approximately $50.90 per task and takes roughly 22 minutes; GPT-5.5 is approximately three times cheaper, while Gemini 3.5 Flash returns a draft in under six minutes. Trace analysis reports average all-pass score differences of +0.4 points for research covering more than 90% of documents, +0.8 for post-draft validation, +1.5 for revision after checking, and +0.3 each for targeted retrieval, structured analysis and returning to source documents. Five or more tool calls in one turn are associated with -0.5 points, and drafting without subsequent validation or revision with -1.2 points. These are reported behavioral associations, not an identified causal intervention. Agent self-checking here is distinct from human verification of AI output. The multi-model deployment recommendation and future research claims are inferences from these results rather than reported tests of production deployments. The supplied text does not state the holdout sample size or uncertainty intervals.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: These are initial findings as of May 26, 2026, conditional on the tested models, agent configurations, task distribution and strict all-pass standard; future improvements have no specified completion date.
pts.d: The authors frame the results as a first look following LAB's release earlier that month. The low completion rates concern complex, long-horizon legal-agent tasks on the tested holdout, not all possible legal assistance or individual subtasks. Agents operate within six available actions: Read, Search, Execute, Write, Validate and Edit. Rankings differ by practice area, and production suitability is conditional on customers' monetary and latency budgets. The authors describe the frontier as improving rapidly but give no date for reliable end-to-end legal work. They announce plans to expand task families, practice areas, context lengths and adjacent professional-service workflows, partner with Artificial Analysis on a regularly updated leaderboard, and collaborate with model providers. Their claim that behavioral analysis will grow in importance is prospective rather than an achieved deployment outcome.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The implications concern lawyers across specialist practices, customers commissioning legal-agent work, and developers and researchers building agents for legal services.
pts.d: Lawyers and legal-service organisations face agents whose capabilities vary by substantive practice and whose outputs rarely satisfy every benchmark requirement. The authors' practical recommendation is to match models to work types rather than treat one model as universally best. Customers' willingness to pay per task and wait for drafts constrains deployable systems. Developers, model providers and researchers are urged to improve model selection, agent workflows, self-correction, domain knowledge, efficiency and behavioral interpretability. Associates serve as the authors' comparison for effective research, drafting, checking and revision workflows, not as the subject of a quantified displacement prediction. The document does not distinguish effects by law-firm size, in-house department or ALSP, and offers no concrete prediction about staffing reductions, billing-model change or access to justice.
